description: I’m a solo participant with a background in cloud engineering, DevOps, cybersecurity, and data-driven prototyping
summary:
LunaMap is an interactive map that helps people explore and compare landing sites near the Moon’s south pole.

Choosing where to land is not just about location. Timing matters too. A site that works well for one mission window may be less suitable if the landing date changes.

Using NASA/JPL Horizons data, LunaMap lets users compare Sun and Earth visibility across different sites and dates. Users can explore the Moon, compare mission priorities, and see how changing the landing window affects which sites meet their requirements. Interactive visualizations also help explain the geometry behind the results.

Our goal is to make lunar landing-site comparisons faster and easier to understand, especially when mission plans change. Rather than replacing NASA’s scientific tools, LunaMap helps turn complex data into information that mission planners, students, and the public can explore.
details:
1. Introduction

I chose the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge because I was curious about how landing dates affect missions near the Moon's south pole. The Sun and Earth often stay close to the horizon in this region. A change in mission timing can make a difference to the conditions at a landing site.

NASA provides tools such as JPL Horizons and Moon Trek, but comparing different locations and dates can take some effort. I started with a simple idea: What if we could explore potential landing sites on the Moon the way we explore places on Google Maps? That idea became LunaMap.

Figure 1. LunaMap's interactive lunar map.

2. What exactly does it do?

LunaMap helps users explore potential lunar landing sites and compare their Sun and Earth visibility over time.

2.1 Explore

The Moon is the main workspace. Users can:

  • Rotate and zoom into the Moon.
  • Search for lunar locations or coordinates.
  • Inspect known sites and nearby landmarks.
  • Select sites for comparison.
  • Switch between map layers.
  • Change the time to see how the Sun's direction affects the view.

Users can also inspect coordinates at other locations. However, visibility statistics are only available for sites that have been analyzed.

Figure 2. Exploring the lunar south pole.

2.2 Compare landing sites

Users can compare up to three analyzed sites. The comparison has three priorities:

  • Sun visibility: Time the Sun stays above the geometric horizon.
  • Earth visibility: Time Earth stays above the geometric horizon.
  • Sun + Earth overlap: Time both are visible at once.

Changing the priority updates the site ranking. Each site also shows visibility durations, continuous intervals and key differences from other selected sites. Moreover, LunaMap lists the advantages and risks for each site for mission planners.

Figures 3–4. Changing the mission priority changes how sites are ranked.

2.3 Mission Window

A landing site may have different conditions depending on the mission date. Users can switch between seven precomputed and validated mission windows. Other supported date ranges can be analyzed through the backend.

Generated results are saved for later use.

2.4 Mission Brief

Mission Brief lets users describe their visibility requirements. For example:

  • Require at least 15 days of Sun visibility.
  • Among sites meeting that requirement, maximize Earth visibility.

LunaMap checks the analyzed sites against these conditions. Users can then change the mission window and evaluate the same requirements again.

Figure 5. Checking landing sites against mission requirements.

2.5 Geometry

Geometry shows the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the Moon and a selected landing site. It provides three views:

  • Sun, Moon and Earth.
  • The Moon and the site.
  • At the site.

The views share one timeline and can play together. This helps explain why the Sun or Earth becomes visible or disappears below the geometric horizon.

Figure 6-1. View of sun, earth and moon relationship

Figure 6-2. Three views of the same moment.

3. How does it work?

3.1 Landing-site selection

For this prototype, I selected four potential landing sites near the lunar south pole from a 2026 research paper.

  • HW06 — Haworth: 87.050° S, 24.240° W
  • MMA01 — Mons Malapert: 85.942° S, 0.944° W
  • MMA04 — Mons Malapert: 86.310° S, 0.459° W
  • MMO03 — Mons Mouton: 85.409° S, 30.406° E

The coordinates come from Wueller et al. (2026), published in Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets. Using sites from the same study provides a consistent starting point for comparison. These are research locations, not confirmed NASA landing destinations.

3.2 Scientific data

LunaMap uses:

  • NASA/JPL Horizons: Sun and Earth positions over time.
  • Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA): Lunar elevation data.
  • NASA Moon Trek: Geographic and terrain references.

3.3 Visibility calculations

The main analysis uses an ideal geometric horizon. An object is considered visible when its apparent elevation is above 0°. LunaMap calculates:

  • Total Sun visibility.
  • Total Earth visibility.
  • Continuous visibility intervals.
  • Sun and Earth visibility overlap.
  • Visibility transitions.

The datasets use 15-minute sampling intervals.

Figure 7. From scientific data to landing-site comparisons.

3.4 System Architecture

LunaMap runs on AWS EC2 using Docker Compose. The system includes:

  • Caddy: Handles HTTPS connections.
  • nginx: Serves the web application and forwards API requests.
  • Python FastAPI: Handles Mission Brief evaluations and analysis requests.
  • Python Worker: Processes new mission-window analyses using NASA/JPL Horizons.
  • Persistent Storage: Stores job records and generated datasets using SQLite and a shared directory.

The API and Worker communicate through shared storage rather than direct network requests. Seven precomputed mission windows are included with the application. New analyses run in the background, and their validated results are saved for later use.

Figure 8. LunaMap's deployment and analysis architecture.

4. Results and validation

4.1 Same sites, different dates

One of LunaMap's main goals is to demonstrate how changing the landing window can change which sites meet the same mission requirements.

We evaluated the same four landing sites across two mission windows, using identical requirements:

Mission requirements:

  • Minimum Sun visibility: At least 15 days during the selected mission window.
  • Optimization objective: Among sites that meet the Sun visibility requirement, select the site with the longest total Earth visibility.

Mission Window 1: 20 Nov – 21 Dec 2025

  • Qualified sites: 4 of 4.
  • Best match: MMA01.
  • Earth visibility: 17.9 days.

Mission Window 2: 20 Jul – 20 Aug 2026

  • Qualified sites: 1 of 4.
  • Best match: MMO03.
  • Earth visibility: 18.0 days.

Key finding: With the same four sites and identical mission requirements, changing only the landing window reduces the number of qualifying sites from four to one and changes the best match from MMA01 to MMO03.

This demonstrates LunaMap's central idea: Same sites. Different landing window. Different answer.

Figures 9–10. Changing the landing window changes which sites meet the same requirements.

4.2 Verification

We checked the geometric analysis for consistency and reproducibility.

Results:

  • Seven precomputed windows reproduced from archived Horizons responses.
  • Visibility-overlap checks passed across seven datasets.
  • Frontend and backend Mission Brief results matched in 42 of 42 tests.
  • All backend tests passed (14 passed, 1 skipped).
  • Additional mission windows were generated and validated through the analysis service.

These checks support the consistency of the geometric calculations. They do not establish that a site is safe or suitable for an actual landing.

4.3 Experimental terrain analysis

We also explored a terrain-aware visibility model using lunar elevation data.

The results can change with small differences in observer position or height. This model has not been validated as thoroughly as the geometric model.

For this reason, terrain-aware results are marked Experimental. They are kept separate from the main rankings and Mission Brief decisions.

5. What benefits does it have?

LunaMap makes it easier to compare landing-site conditions without working through several scientific tools.

Possible uses include:

  • Early mission planning: Compare candidate locations.
  • Schedule changes: Recheck conditions when landing dates change.
  • Mission discussions: Give science and engineering teams a shared visual reference.
  • Education: Explain why sunlight and Earth visibility matter on the Moon.

LunaMap is intended for early comparisons. Detailed mission planning still requires additional engineering analysis.

6. Limitations

LunaMap is a prototype. Its results should be understood within the following limits:

  • Geometric horizon: The main model does not account for terrain blocking the Sun or Earth.
  • Solar power: Sun visibility is not a calculation of power generation.
  • Communications: Earth visibility does not guarantee a working radio link.
  • Terrain-aware model: Experimental and not fully validated.
  • Custom coordinates: Users can inspect locations, but visibility analysis is not available automatically for every coordinate.
  • Map lighting: The Sun's direction changes with time. Terrain-cast shadows are not simulated.

These distinctions are also noted in the application.

7. What do I hope to achieve?

My original idea was to build something like Google Maps for the Moon. I wanted to make lunar landing-site information easier to explore, especially for people who are not familiar with scientific software. For mission teams, LunaMap could serve as a starting point for comparing options. It could also help students understand some of the challenges of exploring the Moon.

There is still more work to do. Future improvements could include better terrain validation and direct analysis of custom coordinates.

For now, LunaMap demonstrates how NASA data can help people compare landing sites through a visual interface.

8. Tools, Languages and Infrastructure

Scientific Data

  • NASA/JPL Horizons — Sun and Earth ephemeris data
  • Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) — Lunar elevation data
  • NASA Moon Trek — Geographic and terrain references

Frontend

  • JavaScript (Vanilla JS)
  • HTML5 and CSS3
  • HTML Canvas and SVG

The interactive Moon and other visualizations were implemented using JavaScript without third-party visualization libraries.

Backend and Analysis

  • Python
  • FastAPI, Pydantic and Uvicorn
  • NumPy and SciPy
  • tifffile
  • SQLite

Deployment

  • AWS EC2 (Ubuntu)
  • Docker and Docker Compose
  • nginx
  • Caddy
  • Git and GitHub

11. Use of SI Tools

LunaMap originated from my idea of building a Google Earth-style interface for exploring and comparing lunar landing sites. I defined the core concept, product requirements, scientific approach, and mission decision workflow. ChatGPT and Claude supported brainstorming, technical research, interface design, coding, debugging, testing, and documentation.

SI tools (Claude and ChatGPT) were used extensively in software development, including code generation and implementation. They also assisted with visual materials and demo video production, including synthetic narration.

I was responsible for the project direction, technical decisions, AWS EC2 infrastructure setup and deployment, scientific validation, and final review. Scientific results were computed from NASA/JPL Horizons data and cross-checked through a separate calculation.

LunaMap does not use SI models to calculate landing-site visibility or generate mission recommendations at runtime.
